techniques.name: Flutter Tongue
techniques.desc:
Produced by rolling an "r" (through the throat or tongue ) while playing. The effect is a rapid fluctuation of tone colour without significant pitch change. 
Speaks best in the middle register at mf and above. 
The tongue one is normally louder than the throat one, but the throat one can be controlled better in all registers, specially piano one.
techniques.composer: Notate with three tremolo strokes plus "flz." and mark clearly where it ends. Reliable down to about C4; below that it becomes dense and less stable.
techniques.oboist:
Doing scales and warm-up with rolled R (tongue) can be really great for your airflow and embouchure, at least is one of my favourite exercises to relax my body before playing and enter a flow action.
One trick is to focus the power of the embouchure on the side of the lips and not on the top/down, giving space for the tongue to freely roll and the air to go through. It takes some training but I love how much expressive the flutter tongue can become after.

techniques.name: Multiphonics
techniques.sub: Two or more pitches at once
techniques.desc:
Special fingerings and embouchure adjustments make the reed vibrate in several modes at once, producing chords, beatings and rough textures. Each multiphonic has its own fingering, dynamic window and degree of stability.
We can divide multiphonics in some categories: honky (the loud ones), beating ones, metamorphic ones (the ones who transform themselves) and double harmonics.
techniques.composer:
I recommend always including a fingering chart for each multiphonic, along with the primary pitch or intended sonority, in the performance notes. On one hand, this allows any performer (regardless of their background in contemporary music) to play the piece easily; on the other hand, if a given fingering fails to produce the desired result, it provides a benchmark to guide them in finding an alternative. I also find it crucial to cite the source index for each multiphonic (for instance, the catalog number from Peter Veale's book), as this helps the performer troubleshoot fingering issues.

When writing a sequence of multiphonics, it is especially important to consider the complexity of fingering transitions. Multiphonics that only require adjustments across the six main tone holes are generally easy to shift between smoothly. However, fingerings that rely heavily on the pinky keys or trill keys can be quite difficult to connect fluidly. Always specify your priorities (such as pitch accuracy, tempo, or dynamics) in the introductory notes so the performer can choose the most effective solutions. Although this level of detail may seem overwhelming, providing this information reduces friction with the score and fosters a better connection between the performer and the piece—often encouraging them to find creative alternatives that benefit the music. Keep in mind that every oboist uses a unique setup (instrument, and reed structure). Therefore, a solution crafted for one player may not work for another. Clear compositional guidelines are essential for finding viable alternatives and making new scores more accessible to musicians of all levels.

Reeds are another crucial consideration. A reed optimized for quiet multiphonics (often referred to as double harmonics) is rarely ideal for produce loud, strongly beating sonorities. This does not mean these contrasting techniques cannot coexist in the same work; rather, composers should temper their expectations to allow each effect to speak in its optimal form.

Consider the mechanics: a loud, beating multiphonic requires a freer-vibrating reed setup to generate the maximum number of partials from a given fingering. Conversely, a double harmonic depends on precise acoustic resonance around a primary pitch. Achieving this delicate balance at a piano dynamic requires greater resistance from the setup—paired with embouchure control aka strong lips —to dampen excess vibration and stabilize the overtone.
techniques.oboist:
While an all-purpose setup does not exist, several key factors can guide the selection process. Starting with a free-vibrating, comfortable reed (one that is neither overly stiff nor brand new) is ideal. 
As a rule of thumb, a balanced reed suited for standard chamber repertoire (such as a wind quintet) serves as a reliable baseline when testing various multiphonics.

Beyond their musical application, multiphonics are an excellent tool for developing vocal-tract awareness and bodily control. Because isolating or emphasizing specific partials within a multiphonic requires adjusting the throat, soft palate, and tongue position, players can incorporate them into their daily warm-ups. Selecting a single multiphonic and attempting to manipulate its partials and dynamic range purely through embouchure, voicing, or oral cavity adjustments offers valuable control over core woodwind mechanics.
techniques.fun: Over 200 oboe multiphonics have been cataloged, yet every reed favors a distinct subset—meaning no two oboists share the same working palette. A single multiphonic can sound vastly different between the beginning and the end of a practice session, dictated simply by variations in embouchure tension and fatigue. For composers seeking strict consistency—where every performance sounds identical—this instability can be frustrating. Reeds seem to exercise a mind of their own, altering the dynamic range or speakability of a multiphonic in response to ambient humidity and room acoustics. Naturally, experienced oboists employ various adjustments to minimize these discrepancies across performances.

techniques.name: Harmonics
techniques.desc: Overblown fingerings that produce a thin, veiled version of the pitch — a flute-like whisper of the note. Available roughly from C5 upward, sounding an octave or a twelfth above the base fingering.
techniques.composer: Notate with a small circle above the note. Best at pp–p dynamic range; harmonics will not project over a full ensemble or orchestra and any try of playing them louder can lead to the harmonics to not speak anymore.
techniques.oboist: Half-hole and voicing control are everything. Think of blowing "through" the note rather than at it.
techniques.fun: Orchestral oboists have quietly used harmonic fingerings for centuries — as secret pianissimo alternatives long before new music asked for them by name.

techniques.name: Circular Breathing
techniques.desc: The player inhales through the nose while pushing air stored in the cheeks through the reed, sustaining the sound indefinitely. The oboe needs so little air that it is one of the friendliest instruments for this.
techniques.composer: You may write phrases of any length — but mark "circular breathing" in the part and expect a small colour ripple at each switch.
techniques.oboist: Start with a straw in a glass of water. The switch is easiest on stable middle-register notes, away from register breaks.
techniques.fun: Heinz Holliger sustained single notes for minutes on end — the oboe uses so little air that one cheekful covers several switches.

techniques.name: Glissando
techniques.desc: A continuous slide produced by gradually sliding fingers off the keys, combined with embouchure bending. Ascending glissandi are easier than descending; the key mechanism limits the usable range.
techniques.composer: Keep glissandi within a third for reliability, and prefer upward slides. Above the staff, the mechanism makes continuous sliding patchy.
techniques.oboist: Slide the fingers sideways off the ring keys while relaxing the jaw. Combining finger and embouchure bend gives the widest smooth slide.
techniques.fun: The famous opening slide of Rhapsody in Blue is a clarinet glissando — the oboe version is much harder, which is exactly why it is fun.

techniques.name: Pitch Bend
techniques.desc: Lipping the pitch up or down — roughly a quarter-tone to a semitone — using embouchure and voicing alone. Ideal for microtonal inflections, "blue" notes and expressive ornaments.
techniques.composer: Quarter-tone bends are safe anywhere; a full semitone only works in the middle register at moderate dynamics.
techniques.oboist: Drop the jaw and lower the tongue to bend down — think "ee" to "aw". Bending up is much harder; approach from below instead.
techniques.fun: Baroque oboists bent pitch constantly as a matter of style — equal temperament is younger than the instrument itself.

techniques.name: Key Clicks
techniques.desc: The keys are slapped without blowing — or with air only — turning the oboe into a quiet percussion instrument with faint pitch shadows of the fingerings.
techniques.composer: Very quiet — amplify, or score them in silence. Use x-noteheads at the fingering pitch to control the colour of each click.
techniques.oboist: The low C, B and B♭ keys give the loudest clicks. Adding a breathy "huh" of air doubles the presence.
techniques.fun: Unamplified key clicks carry barely ten metres in a hall — intimacy is the whole point of the effect.

techniques.name: Air Sounds
techniques.desc: Blowing air through the instrument without engaging the reed — from pure white-noise breath to half-tone mixtures where a shadow of pitch appears inside the noise.
techniques.composer: Notate air with a triangle notehead and specify the consonant — "ss", "ff" or "sh" — since each filters the noise differently.
techniques.oboist: Loosen the embouchure until the reed just stops speaking; the fingering still colours the noise, so change fingerings expressively.
techniques.fun: The oboe’s narrow bore makes its air sounds the most "whistly" of all the woodwinds.

techniques.name: Cor Anglais: Low Register
techniques.sub: The dark voice of the cor anglais
techniques.desc: The bottom fifth of the cor anglais — written B3 down to E3, sounding a fifth lower — has a covered, reedy darkness the oboe cannot reach. Slow to speak, enormous in colour.
techniques.composer: Approach the lowest notes by step and give them time — attacks below written G3 are slow at pp. Unbeatable for lament-like solos.
techniques.oboist: Use a slightly heavier reed and think warm, slow air. Practise pp attacks daily; they are this register’s whole craft.
techniques.fun: The cor anglais is neither English nor a horn — "anglais" is probably a corruption of "anglé" (angled), after its old curved shape.

techniques.name: Single-tonguing
techniques.desc: Single-tonguing is the default articulation on oboe, striking each note with a single tongue stroke against the reed, usually near the tip. It is the baseline every other articulation gets compared against.
techniques.composer: Reliable across the full range and every dynamic, no caveats needed. That is exactly what makes it a poor showcase on its own, but the natural default for anything that is not asking for another articulation.
techniques.oboist: The real work is consistency: same syllable, same placement, same air support across registers and dynamics, so a scale does not audibly change character as it climbs.

techniques.name: Double-tonguing
techniques.desc: Double-tonguing splits a fast articulated passage across two syllables, typically "tu-ku" or "ta-ka", so the tongue and the back of the tongue alternate the attack instead of a single stroke repeating over and over. It lets fast repeated notes go beyond what single-tonguing can sustain without tiring.
techniques.composer: Once secure, it removes speed as a limiting factor for repeated notes and rapid articulation, opening tempos well beyond comfortable single-tonguing range. It tends to hold up best in the middle register at moderate to loud dynamics; very soft dynamics or extreme registers make the "ku" syllable harder to match cleanly to the "tu".
techniques.oboist: The two syllables need to sound identical in weight and length before speed matters at all. Most players default to a slightly weaker "ku" without noticing. Practising slowly with a metronome, listening specifically for the second syllable, beats practising fast.

techniques.name: Triple-tonguing
techniques.desc: Triple-tonguing extends the double-tonguing pattern to groups of three, typically "tu-tu-ku" or "ta-ta-ka", matching triplet subdivisions at speed.
techniques.composer: Useful specifically for fast triplet or compound metre passages where double-tonguing’s two-syllable pattern does not divide evenly. Reliability tracks closely with how solid the double-tonguing already is, since it is built from the same syllable pair.
techniques.oboist: The trap is letting the pattern drift into "tu-ku-tu, ku-tu-ku" across the barline instead of a clean "tu-tu-ku" repeated, which changes the accent pattern audibly. Isolating the syllable order away from the actual notes fixes it faster than practising on the passage itself.

techniques.name: Slap-tongue
techniques.desc: Slap-tongue creates a dry, percussive attack by building suction between the tongue and the reed, then releasing it sharply. More a mechanical pop than a blown note.
techniques.composer: Works as a genuinely percussive colour, closer to a woodblock than an oboe attack, and reads clearly even in a dense texture because it does not rely on sustained air. Reliability drops in extreme registers where reed response is already unstable.
techniques.oboist: It is a suction and release action, not a hit. Players who try to hit the reed harder usually get an inconsistent result. Isolating the tongue and reed contact away from full embouchure pressure first makes the mechanism clearer before adding pitch.

techniques.name: Playing with the Reed Only
techniques.sub: The raw crow of the reed
techniques.desc: Removing the instrument and playing on the reed alone exposes its raw "crow", the buzzing sound it makes on its own before the oboe’s bore shapes it into a note.
techniques.composer: Useful as a distinct, exposed timbre rather than an oboe substitute. Reliability depends heavily on the individual reed, since reed response varies more here than through the full instrument.
techniques.oboist: Closer to reed testing than performance technique, so the same care that goes into checking a reed’s crow translates directly. Recording it separately, rather than cutting to it live, avoids an awkward instrument-removal moment.

techniques.name: Special Effects without the Reed
techniques.desc: The inverse: removing the reed and playing the bare instrument, relying on breath and key noise without any reed vibration.
techniques.composer: Produces a hollow, breathy, unpitched character, essentially air tones and key noise without any reed content at all. Reliable as a texture, unreliable as anything resembling a pitched note.
techniques.oboist: Worth recording as its own isolated sound rather than a live switch mid-performance; removing the reed cleanly during a piece is a practical hazard, not a musical one.

techniques.name: Vibrato
techniques.desc: Vibrato oscillates pitch and intensity around a sustained note through controlled diaphragm or throat pulsing. The oboe’s core expressive device rather than an extended technique.
techniques.composer: Depth and speed are both adjustable and can be notated as parameters (slow/wide versus fast/narrow) rather than left constant. Holds up reliably across the full range and most dynamics, though very soft high notes narrow the room to vary depth without destabilising pitch.
techniques.oboist: Depth and speed are worth practising as independent variables; most players default to one habitual vibrato and never test the edges of the range on purpose. Comparing it at extreme dynamics shows where it needs the most conscious control.

techniques.name: Lip Glissando
techniques.desc: A lip glissando bends pitch through embouchure and lip tension alone, without changing fingering, producing a smaller, smoother slide than a full fingered glissando.
techniques.composer: The interval range is narrow, closer to a pitch bend than a real glide between distant notes, so it works best as an ornament on a single fingering rather than a way to connect two different notes. Strongest in the middle register.
techniques.oboist: The slide should come from gradually loosening or tightening the lips, not from the jaw; jaw movement destabilises tone quality fast. Practising the two endpoints in isolation before connecting them makes the motion more controlled.

techniques.name: Smorzato
techniques.desc: Smorzato fades a note out gradually while keeping its pitch centred, rather than simply decrescendoing to silence. The pitch stays locked as the sound thins.
techniques.composer: A controlled disappearance rather than a stop, useful at phrase endings where a normal diminuendo would read as too final or too gradual a change in colour. Depends on register: very high or low notes are harder to keep centred as air support drops.
techniques.oboist: The temptation is to let pitch drift flat as air drops, which defeats the effect. Keeping voicing and support active even as volume falls is the real skill.

techniques.name: Oscillato
techniques.desc: Oscillato produces a controlled pitch wobble through embouchure movement, distinct from vibrato in that the oscillation is usually wider and slower, closer to a deliberate pitch wave than an expressive shimmer.
techniques.composer: Works as a distinct effect from vibrato when notated separately, wider and more deliberate rather than blended into the tone. Extreme widths risk losing the fundamental pitch reference entirely.
techniques.oboist: Isolating oscillato from habitual vibrato takes conscious effort since the muscles involved overlap; practising the two side by side rather than in isolation helps.

techniques.name: Singing and Humming
techniques.desc: Singing or humming a pitch while playing a different note produces two simultaneous voices, the sung tone and the played tone, rather than a single line.
techniques.composer: Genuinely polyphonic from a single performer, and the interval between sung and played pitch is a real compositional parameter. Close intervals are harder to keep independent than wide ones.
techniques.oboist: Balancing volume between the two lines takes real practice; one usually dominates by default. Starting with the pitches far apart makes the coordination easier before narrowing the interval.

techniques.name: Vocalisation
techniques.desc: Vocalisation lets the voice and instrument interact without singing a distinct separate pitch, closer to speaking, growling, or shaping vowels through the instrument than producing two independent notes.
techniques.composer: More textural and less strictly pitched than singing and humming, useful for vocal-adjacent colour rather than genuine two-voice writing. More aggressive vocal effects are harder to sustain over a long phrase.
techniques.oboist: Forcing the throat for a stronger effect tends to backfire and costs endurance fast. A lighter vocal effort usually reads just as clearly through the instrument.

techniques.name: Loudest Note in the Multiphonic
techniques.desc: Every multiphonic fingering produces several simultaneous pitches at different volumes. This isolates and brings out the loudest component through air support and voicing.
techniques.composer: The most audible, foreground pitch within a given multiphonic chord, useful as the primary melodic reference point when writing multiphonics into a line. Some multiphonics have a much clearer dominant pitch than others.
techniques.oboist: Finding it is a listening exercise as much as a technical one, isolating each component of the chord by ear before trying to emphasise one over the others.

techniques.name: Lowest Note in the Multiphonic
techniques.desc: The inverse: isolating and emphasising the lowest pitch within a multiphonic’s chord rather than the loudest overall component.
techniques.composer: Gives access to the multiphonic’s bass note as a distinct, controllable element, useful when the chord’s foundation matters more than its brightest component. Some fingerings have a much steadier low component than others.
techniques.oboist: Tends to need more air support and less brightness in the voicing than emphasising the loudest component, essentially the opposite embouchure adjustment.

techniques.name: Multiphonics with Beats
techniques.desc: Tuning the multiphonic’s component pitches close enough together that they interfere and produce an audible pulsing, or beating, rather than a stable chord.
techniques.composer: The beating rate itself becomes a controllable parameter, faster or slower depending on how closely the components are tuned, genuinely usable as a rhythmic device on its own. Sensitive to reed and embouchure adjustment: small changes shift the rate noticeably.
techniques.oboist: A tuning exercise more than a fingering one; small embouchure adjustments change the beat rate directly. Worth practising slowly with attention to the pulse rather than the pitch.

techniques.name: Multiphonics with High Noise Content
techniques.desc: Pushing a multiphonic toward its noisier, less pitched end, favouring air turbulence over clean pitch content within the chord.
techniques.composer: A genuinely unstable, textural sound, closer to breath noise with harmonic colour than a clean chord, useful where instability is the point rather than a defect. Inherently lower reliability than a clean multiphonic, since noise content is harder to control precisely.
techniques.oboist: Closer to controlled instability than a mistake, worth practising deliberately rather than just noting when a multiphonic happens to come out noisy.

techniques.name: Transitions to the Multiphonics
techniques.desc: Moving from a single pitched tone into a multiphonic fingering without an audible break, connecting the two rather than treating them as separate events.
techniques.composer: Lets a multiphonic emerge from an existing line rather than interrupting it, a real option when the chord needs to feel discovered rather than announced. Some note-to-multiphonic pairs transition far more smoothly than others.
techniques.oboist: The fingering change and any embouchure adjustment need to happen gradually rather than as a single switch; practising the transition in slow motion first makes the seam disappear faster.

techniques.name: Rolling Notes
techniques.sub: Rolling a finger across the hole
techniques.desc: A multiphonic effect produced by rolling a finger gradually across a key or tonehole rather than lifting it cleanly, sliding the chord’s pitch content rather than switching it discretely.
techniques.composer: A genuinely continuous shift in the multiphonic’s character rather than a stepped change, closer to a slow morph than a cut. Reliability drops as roll speed increases: faster rolls are harder to control precisely.
techniques.oboist: Start slow and only increase speed once the slow version is fully controlled. This is one where rushing the practice actively works against the result.

techniques.name: Eighth-tone Scale
techniques.desc: A scale built from eighth-tone steps, using specific microtonal fingerings between the standard chromatic pitches, a finer division than the more familiar quarter-tone.
techniques.composer: Opens a finer microtonal grid than quarter-tones, useful where more than two intermediate steps are needed between adjacent semitones. Depends on consistent fingering choice, since several possible fingerings can approximate the same step with different intonation tendencies.
techniques.oboist: Consistency matters more than perfect tuning; picking one fingering per step and using it every time keeps the scale legible even if individual pitches drift slightly.

techniques.name: Double Harmonics
techniques.desc: Sounding two harmonics of the same fundamental simultaneously, rather than a single harmonic, by carefully balancing air support between the two upper partials.
techniques.composer: A genuinely two-note effect from a single fingering, distinct in colour from a normal dyad since both notes share the same fundamental. Closer harmonics tend to lock in more easily than distant ones.
techniques.oboist: Stabilising the fundamental first, before attempting to add the second harmonic on top, makes the whole thing far more repeatable than trying to find both at once.

techniques.name: Timbre Fingerings
techniques.desc: Alternate fingerings for the same written pitch that change the note’s colour, brightness, or resonance rather than its pitch, letting a single note shift character without moving.
techniques.composer: A genuine colour palette at a fixed pitch, useful for repeated or sustained notes that need to shift character without changing pitch. Some alternates are far more stable in pitch than others despite the colour change.
techniques.oboist: Worth cataloguing which alternates stay truly in tune at the same pitch versus which ones drift slightly, since not every timbral fingering is pitch-neutral.

techniques.name: Trills and Tremolos
techniques.desc: Fast alternation between two fingerings, either adjacent (trill) or more distant (tremolo), including alternates not available through standard trill keys.
techniques.composer: Extends trill and tremolo possibilities beyond the standard fingering system, including intervals or pitches a conventional trill key cannot reach. Some alternate trills are far more even than others.
techniques.oboist: Evenness between the two fingerings matters more than raw speed; an uneven trill reads as sloppy even at a reasonable tempo. Worth practising slowly until both fingerings feel identical in weight.

techniques.name: Teeth Notes
techniques.desc: Bringing the teeth into gentle contact with the reed, adding a buzzing, distorted edge to the tone alongside the normal embouchure.
techniques.composer: A distinct distortion colour layered on top of a normal note rather than replacing it, closer to an added texture than a separate technique. Light contact is more sustainable than heavy contact over a long phrase.
techniques.oboist: Should stay gentle and controlled, more contact than pressure. Forcing it risks reed damage without actually improving the effect.

techniques.name: Alla Tromba
techniques.desc: Shaping the attack and resonance of a note to resemble a trumpet’s character, through a sharper, more focused articulation and embouchure adjustment rather than any fingering change.
techniques.composer: A borrowed brass character on a double reed instrument, useful where a fanfare-like attack is wanted without an actual brass instrument. Holds up best in the middle to upper register, where a sharper attack reads most clearly.
techniques.oboist: The effect comes mostly from the attack, not the sustained tone, so the first few milliseconds of the note deserve more attention than the rest of the phrase.

F, G, B · beating
multiphonics.notes: The multiphonic although is easy to play is really dependent of the embochure to stay stable. Depending of the air pressure one can choose the low or high harmonics of it.

multiphonics.name: A#1, E2, F#3, G#3 · beating
multiphonics.notes: The multiphonic has a small beating but it breaks quite easily, it can of course depend on the reed on use, but it is a multiphonic that doesn't have a lot of dynamic range. The lower and higher note are the most audible

multiphonics.name: F5, C#6, G4 · honky
multiphonics.notes: This multiphonic is quite exciting because although is very stable, it allows to play with air pressure. It also has the potencial of nice multiphonic trills with the half key of d, and the f key on the left hand (n.5)

multiphonics.name: G#, C#6, F#5, D#4 · beating
multiphonics.notes: This multiphonic has some beating to it, and the beating can change the speed depending on the embochure. Although the multiphonics speaks quite well, one has to be careful with changes from this multiphonic to others, since has an half hole, and keys being pressed on both little fingers.

multiphonics.name: G#4, D6, G5, F4 · beating
multiphonics.notes: Depending on the embochure and pressure, the G5 can become a F#5. Due to the half hole/C# key combination it can be a multiphonic that needs a bit of time to prepare

multiphonics.name: G5,F4,D6,A4 · honky
multiphonics.notes: This multiphonic has a lot of trill possiilities, also, depending on the pressure of air and embochure, one can isolate the high G (eh- D)

pairs.label: Advanced — Very Effective
pairs.notes: A continuous, pulsating stream of colour that never breathes. Demands real stamina — stunning in slow builds.

pairs.label: Dense & Turbulent
pairs.notes: A rough, buzzing chord-noise. Only the most stable multiphonics survive the flutter — pick them together with your player.

pairs.label: Seamless — Expressive Gold
pairs.notes: Finger glissando plus embouchure bend covers the widest smooth slides the oboe can make. A natural marriage.

pairs.label: Ghost Machine
pairs.notes: Percussive clicks inside a halo of breath — a whole quiet ensemble from a single player. Amplify for magic.

pairs.label: Fragile — Handle With Care
pairs.notes: Both need precise voicing, and combining them usually collapses one or the other. Alternate rather than superimpose.

pairs.label: Dark Growl
pairs.notes: Flutter in the cor anglais low register is a slow, furry rumble — one of the darkest colours in the double-reed family.

pairs.label: Deep Fog
pairs.notes: Air sounds through the cor anglais are lower and rounder than on oboe — a warm, distant wind. Beautiful in transitions.

pairs.label: Endless Spiral
pairs.notes: An unbroken slide that keeps circling without a breath. Keep the range modest and it hypnotises.

pairs.label: Beating Clouds
pairs.notes: Bending one component of a multiphonic creates slow beating waves — a favourite of spectral writing.

pairs.label: Workable — Rhythmic Grit
pairs.notes: Alternating flutter bursts with key clicks makes a nice grainy groove; superimposing them buries the clicks.

pairs.label: Veiled Whisper
pairs.notes: A harmonic emerging from inside an air sound is one of the most delicate entrances the oboe can make.

pairs.label: Delicate — Narrow Window
pairs.notes: Harmonics can be bent, but only slightly — a few cents of shimmer rather than a true slide.

pairs.label: The Infinite Swarm
pairs.notes: A sustained multiphonic with no breaths — a swarm that never lands. Choose a very stable multiphonic.

faq.q: Can I write to you about a piece I'm composing?
faq.a: Yes, please do! Use the contact form below — tell me about the piece, the techniques you're curious about, and I'll get back to you.

faq.q: Do you record demos of new works?
faq.a: I do. Send me the passage or the technique you want to hear through the contact form and we can arrange a recording.

faq.q: Can I use the sounds on this site in my piece?
faq.a: The demos here are references, not samples. If you'd like real recordings to work with, write to me and we'll sort it out.

faq.q: What's the written range of oboe and cor anglais?
faq.a: Oboe: B♭3 to about G6 (A6 with courage). Cor anglais: written E3–E6, sounding a fifth lower. Extremes get fragile at soft dynamics.
Send a message through the form with your idea, instrumentation and timeline — I'll reply with availability and next steps.

texts.mixSub: Pick two techniques and see how well they get along.
texts.tvSub: Reels, seagull sounds and experiments — zapping encouraged. YouTube and Instagram both play here.
texts.contactSub: Commissions, recordings, questions about a passage you're writing — or just to say your multiphonic finally spoke. Messages land straight in Patrícia's inbox.
texts.footerLine: Curated by Patrícia Pinheiro — oboe & cor anglais
texts.coffeeSub: This playground is built and recorded by one oboist, between rehearsals. A coffee (or a piece of cane) keeps the recordings, the multiphonic analyses and the whole archive growing — and free for everyone.
texts.thanks: This archive grew out of conversations with composers, colleagues and teachers who kept asking for a sound before writing it. Thank you to everyone who lent a reed, an ear or an afternoon of recording — and to the authors below, whose work is the ground every page here stands on.
texts.bibSub: What was used and by whom. Each technique lists the sources behind its description; the full references are here.
